In the southern part of its range, it is black and brown with a white stripe on its face and a white tip on its tail.
The fox squirrel eats acorns, hickory, walnut, beech, mulberry and hawthorne seeds. It also eats green shoots and buds, fruits, berries, corn, insects, moths and beetles. Nuts are stored for use in the winter."(NatureWorks)

I found this Squirrel while I was taking a walk looking for different species. Squirrels are some of the most populated rodents in the country. This squirrel looked like it was on the hunt for food. An interesting fact about squirrels is that they "sometimes pretend to bury a nut to throw off a potential thief." They are extremely fast and agile to avoid predators. They also have fur that will keep them warm in the winter time. In this observation the squirrel is sitting on a fence and most likely planning it's next adventure. This was one of my favorite observations and helped me learn more about this animal.

The past few years of observing these small mammals, have given me a new perspective.  For instance; you know how people ask, "What animal would you most like to be?"  Tiger?  Well, beautiful yes.  But nowadays, you would either be incessantly hunted, or living in a cage.  A bird!  Neat... Soaring in a cloud filled sky!  Sometimes, sure, but have you thought about the predators, or the thousands of miles (in some cases) migrating twice each year.  Not for me.  I have concluded that a well-balanced life has to involve, in some way, the reduction of stress.  And in that category, these furry poppets wear the crown.  Dream on, squirrel.

But eventually we figured it out, and a potentially wasted morning became an enjoyable walk/birding trip. The weather was sunny, hot (especially later and in the sun), and humid, with a light breeze. We started at the trailhead near the softball fields and walked clockwise. At the midway point, we rested and drank liquids from a vending machine; then we continued east, then south, back to Jet. The first half of the walk was through giant oaks and natural wetlands, while the second half was treeless and passed many small retention ponds. We saw 3 separate Sherman's Fox Squirrels -- and ZERO Gray Squirrels! We left at 1225 and headed to lunch at Roberto's Italian Ristorante and Pizzeria -- delicious.

description:
Humor outside my window
Photo 1:
Hey, No Birds, Now's My Chance
Usually the feeder is full of birds but for once it was empty.  The squirrel wanted the food but took the lazy way of reaching it.
Photo 2:
I'll Just Lean Over & Grab A Bite
The epitome of lazy, this squirrel likes to just lean over & go face first in the seed, eating without using paws to hold the food.  Or taking the trouble to jump or climb onto the feeder.
Photo 3:
Yum!  That's Good!
That's a happy squirrel.
Photo 4:
Wonder If I Can Reach That Peanut?
As I watched, he stretched out full length trying to reach an elusive peanut.  At the same time, the feeder started tilting away from him.  
Photo 5:
Just A Leetle Further....
Squirrel on tippy toes stretched further and feeder tilted further away from him.  This was getting interesting.  Squirrel was determined to get that peanut.
Photo 6:
Tiny Bit Further And Whoops!
He kept stretching up on his toes & the feeder kept tilting away from him.  Right after this shot, he slipped and fell off the brick.  Jumped to his feet and ran off.  I was laughing too hard to get a shot.  Doubt he learned anything, he does this frequently.

description:
Today a neighbor 2 houses down had a large mature live oak tree taken down.  I talked to the crew doing the work and said to let me know if they found any nests of babies.  I was thinking birds but what they found was squirrels.  When they came to me, they had put these 4 babies on the trunk of another tree where they could barely hang on and they were crying loudly, a sound that sounded like baby birds, not squirrels.  No parents around and no more home tree for a parent to take them to.  They were too young to be out of the nest and their cries were already attracting a couple of cats.  We also have some very active Cooper's hawks on our street.  If left for parents, I didn't think a mother squirrel could keep all 4 safe with no nest to take them to and predators already waiting.  So I took them to a friend of mine who is a vet and has rehabbed squirrels several times before.  Looks like the mother squirrel may be the same one who had a blond baby squirrel last fall that did well so glad this rare fox squirrel color will be continued. Two of the 4 babies are blond with blue eyes. The person holding the babies here is the vet who was checking them out.  They look to be between 4 and 5 weeks old. Using flash turned the eyes of the blond squirrels pink, although they are actually blue.  The normal colored babies had the normal dark eyes.
They were rehabbed and released

description: I rarely get the chance to come up to McKinney, so I visited a couple parks in the area.

The Red (Pine) squirrel is most common in our area and until recently were nearly always present in our trees. We jokingly have called Fox squirrel, "City squirrels", because while prevalent down in the Boise valley, we had not observed them in the mountains. I first observed a Fox squirrel 2-3 years ago on Montgomery St. in Idaho City. About a year ago, I observed one in our trees and on our deck. Roughly 1/2-3/4 of a mile from where I had seen one on Montgomery St. It appeared one day, then I didn't see another for several months. Pine squirrel were still abundant. Since Jan. 2022, I noticed fewer, then no Pine squirrel. The two cats that adopted us are definitely part of the reason. In the absence of Pine squirrels, I've noted the presence of Fox squirrel more often. Yesterday I observed it appears we have a pair of them that have moved in. 
Also, seems the Fox squirrel is not the jabberbox the Pine squirrel is. Pine squirrel seem to chatter nearly constantly. Until this morning, I hadn't heard the Fox squirrel make a sound. One I was watching this morning barked a bit. Seemingly to alert that one of the cats was in the open.
As well as being far less vocal than Pine squirrel, the Fox squirrel is approximately 1/3 larger, the tail is roughly equal to body length and tail movements are less twitchy and more fluid. The Fox squirrel tail appears more evenly covered with fur. Fur of Pine squirrel tails can appear a bit thin and scraggly.

description: Plants and critters from Weymouth Woods, Moore County, NC (USA). Fox Squirrel - Sciurus niger (melanistic), subspecies: Southern Fox Squirrel - Sciurus niger niger I have seen both dark phase and "fox-colored" squirrels at Weymouth Woods. Eastern Gray Squirrels also occur. This squirrel was gnawing avidly on the upper surface of the branch it was perched on (shown in one frame). This is, I think, a fox squirrel and not a melanistic Eastern Gray Squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis). I was not close enough to judge the size in any way. Looking at images on the Internet, Fox Squirrels seem to have a more robust, less-tapered "snout" than Eastern Gray Squirrels. That matches the images here, to my eye. Other features I notice: - Toes of this squirrel are quite robust (and more hairy?) compared to what I have seen in gray squirrels. Toe pads are quite prominent. (That would make sense for a Fox Squirrel, as they are more terrestrial than Gray Squirrels.) - Ears appear to be shorter and more rounded than in Eastern Gray. - Pelage coarse and shaggy. Some of the putative distinctive features noted above are marked in one detail image. Most references just mention the size and pelage to differentiate from Eastern Gray Squirrel. One historical reference has helpful notes on other characters: "A large, arboreal Squirrel of rather variable color pattern - much larger and heavier in build than the Eastern Gray Squirrels; pelage coarse and harsh; hands and feet large, soles naked; nose and ears always white." - Anthony, Field Book of North American Mammals, 1928, p. 275 (BHL link)

The Fox Squirrel (Sciurus niger)  is an active and self-dependent species that can mostly be seen in either pairs or alone. These squirrels are the largest species of tree squirrels in the US. They are also considered an invasive species given the nature and frequency of their sightings. Fox squirrels are omnivores and have a varying diet, but mostly eat nuts, flowers, and buds that reside in oak trees. They do well in open and spaced-out areas, which is probably why so many are at the Claremont Colleges; for open space and also the well spaced-out trees as well. These squirrels also use trees to escape from common predators like bobcats, coyotes, hawks, and owls. Because squirrels are so agile in trees, it is easy for them to avoid predators there.

description: The Sciurus Niger, also known as the fox squirrel, is a common squirrel species native to North America, and it is heavily populated in Southern California. This image of a fox squirrel was photographed on the campus of Pitzer College, showing an example of biodiversity in an urban environment. This species primarily lives in the trees planted throughout the Claremont Colleges and on a broader scale, they live in forest and tree habitats throughout the central and eastern parts of North America. While these squirrels are more abundant in the wild such as pine forests and oak trees, they can commonly be found in urban ecosystems due to the present biodiversity in cities. The diet of these fox squirrels can range from insects and birds to seeds and nuts, as they are omnivores. On the other side of the food chain, they are hunted by predators including owls and hawks. The population of these species is at a strong number of 20,000, and there is no present concern of extinction for these species.
